procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The text does not explicitly mention any High Court proceedings. It implies that the petitioner directly approached the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner initially sent an application to the Supreme Court requesting to be produced before it to challenge his detention. The Court treated this application as a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution and issued a rule nisi. The petitioner was allowed to file a comprehensive amended petition after applying to raise additional grounds. The State filed multiple affidavits in reply. Ultimately, the petition failed and was dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the amending Act was validly assented to by the Governor.

facts: The Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir was amended by the (Sixth Amendment) Act, 1965, which replaced the office of the elected 'Sadar-i-Riyasat' with that of an appointed 'Governor' as the Head of State.
An amending Act was subsequently passed and received assent from the Governor.

The validity of this Act was challenged on the grounds that the Governor was not the proper authority to give assent, as the original constitutional provisions referred specifically to the Sadar-i-Riyasat.
law: Section 18 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir provides that the General Clauses Act shall apply for the interpretation of the Constitution.
The legal principle of succession, as supported by the General Clauses Act, allows a successor to an office to exercise the powers of the predecessor.
Sections 26, 27, and 28 of the Jammu and Kashmir Constitution define the Head of the State and vest executive powers in that office.
application: The Court rejected the argument that the Constitution required the perpetual existence of the Sadar-i-Riyasat for giving assent.
It reasoned that the Governor is the legal successor to the Sadar-i-Riyasat. Both offices represent the Head of the State.

By applying the General Clauses Act (as mandated by Section 18 of the J&K Constitution), the Court found that the Governor, as the successor, is entitled to exercise all the powers previously held by the Sadar-i-Riyasat, including the power to assent to bills.

The Court clarified that the change was merely in the designation and mode of appointment of the Head of State (from elected Sadar-i-Riyasat to appointed Governor) and did not fundamentally alter the character of the responsible government.
Since the office of Sadar-i-Riyasat no longer existed, any constitutional reference to it must now be interpreted as a reference to its successor, the Governor.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the Governor was the legal successor to the Sadar-i-Riyasat and was therefore fully competent to give assent. Consequently, the amending Act was validly assented to by the Governor.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds on which the detenu has been detained have relevance to the security of the State.

facts: The detenu was detained on grounds that were not disclosed to him, with the state claiming it was against the public interest to do so.
The detenu argued that the real grounds for his detention might have no relation to the security of the State.
The State produced the file containing the grounds of detention before the High Court for its review.
law: The Supreme Court established that the Preventive Detention Act does not prevent the High Court or the Supreme Court from reviewing the validity of a detention.
The courts have the jurisdiction to call upon the State to produce the grounds of detention and other materials to satisfy themselves that the detention is lawful and in accordance with the Act.
application: The Court exercised its power to review the confidential file that the State had produced before the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: After examining the file, the Court was satisfied that the grounds on which the detenu had been detained were, in fact, relevant to the security of the State. This finding also led the court to reject the related argument that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the case.

issue.issue_text: Whether the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts of the case.

facts: The petitioner's counsel, Mr. Garg, raised the point that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts of the case.
application: The Court first examined the grounds on which the person was detained.
The Court found that the grounds for detention were relevant to the security of the State.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the Court was satisfied that the grounds for detention were relevant to state security, it concluded that the argument that the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts of the case must also fail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the amending Act was validly assented to by the Governor.
appellant_arguments: The only way to modify Article 370 is as specified in Article 370(3) itself, implying that the amendment which replaced the Sadar-i-Riyasat with a Governor was invalid, and therefore the Governor's subsequent assent was not valid.
respondent_arguments: The Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir (Sixth Amendment) Act, 1965, which had received the assent of the Sadar-i-Riyasat, validly amended the Constitution of Jammu & Kashmir, validly provided for the appointment of a Governor, and therefore, the Governor was competent to give assent to the Act in question.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grounds on which the detenu has been detained have relevance to the security of the State.
appellant_arguments: The grounds for detention are not relevant to the security of the State.
respondent_arguments: The grounds for detention are relevant to the security of the State, as evidenced by the file produced before the court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts of the case.
appellant_arguments: The detaining authority had not applied its mind to the facts of the case.
respondent_arguments: The detaining authority did apply its mind to the facts of the case.

cases.case_name: A. K. Gopalan v. The State of Madras
cases.principle: Cited for the point that Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act was struck down.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A proviso in an act is not ultra vires if the proviso and the act do not bar the High Court or this Court from looking into the validity of the detention.
obiter: When a detaining authority makes a direction, it cannot be said that the detaining authority is exercising any legislative power.
The grounds on which a person has been detained must have relevance to the security of the State.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court upheld the detention, finding that the amending Act under which the detention was ordered was validly assented to by the Governor, whose position was a legitimate change in designation from the Sadar-i-Riyasat. Furthermore, after a direct review of the confidential file produced by the State, the court was satisfied that the grounds for detention were relevant to the security of the State, which in turn demonstrated that the detaining authority had applied its mind to the case.
legal_tests_applied: Direct judicial review of the confidential grounds and materials for detention to satisfy the court that the detention is in accordance with law and that the grounds are relevant to the stated purpose (e.g., security of the State).
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that changing the head of state's designation from Sadar-i-Riyasat to Governor was an invalid constitutional change, viewing it instead as a permissible alteration similar to the one that had earlier created the office of Sadar-i-Riyasat.
The appellant's assertion that the detention grounds were irrelevant to state security was contradicted by the court's own examination of the confidential file produced by the State.

The argument that the detaining authority failed to apply its mind was dismissed as a direct consequence of the court finding the detention grounds to be relevant; the relevance of the grounds implied that the authority had properly considered the facts.
why_respondent_won: The State successfully argued that the change in designation from Sadar-i-Riyasat to Governor was a valid constitutional amendment, making the Governor's assent to the subsequent Act legitimate.

By producing the confidential file for the court's inspection, the State enabled the court to independently satisfy itself that the grounds for detention were directly relevant to the security of the State.
The court's satisfaction with the relevance of the detention grounds served as sufficient proof that the detaining authority had applied its mind, thereby validating the respondent's position.
policy_considerations: The court's power of judicial review is essential to ensure detentions are lawful. The court explicitly noted that the Act in question was sustainable precisely because it did not bar the High Court or Supreme Court from calling upon the State to produce the grounds of detention and other materials to verify the legality of the detention.
